You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel – Buyer-Side Review of Seller's SPA Update and Disclosure Letter

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Date:** 5 November 2026
**Scope:** Seller Update (key positions) and Disclosure Letter SPA-003 (dated 22 September 2026)

---

## 1. Headline view

The Seller's package is materially seller-favourable and, in several places, internally inconsistent with the Seller's own Disclosure Letter. The Disclosure Letter is actually quite candid — it repeatedly admits that consents, discharges, payments and investigations are *not* complete — while the Seller Update treats each of those same matters as resolved, immaterial or "ordinary course". That gap is where the risk sits for Wattlebridge.

Two threshold points before the detail:

**(a) The "Preamble" should be disregarded as a negotiating device.** It asserts that the positions are "FINAL", "settled at principal level" and "not intended to be re-opened". We have no record from the Wattlebridge side that these points were agreed by our principals; the Seller's counsel cannot bind us by labelling their own draft as agreed. The market-terms assertions are also one-sided (they cite only the seller-friendly end of each range). Please confirm with the Wattlebridge principals whether anything in Clauses 8, 12 or 13 was actually agreed commercially. Absent that confirmation, treat every point as open.

**(b) The Disclosure Letter is stale.** It speaks as at 5.00pm on 22 September 2026 — over six weeks ago. Several disclosed matters (Bluefen consent, Riverlark discharge, Ironquay payment, the DD-006 incident) are time-sensitive and were expressly incomplete at that date. We need a bring-down disclosure and updated data room before signing, and again at Completion.

---

## 2. Issue-by-issue analysis

### Issue 1 – Liability cap (Cl 12.1): 20% / AUD 4.8m

**Seller position:** Aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims capped at AUD 4,800,000.

**Why it matters:** The identified exposures alone (Riverlark AUD 3.2m, Bluefen revenue ~AUD 3.6m p.a., bonuses AUD 420k, Ironquay AUD 180k+, Sandbar AUD 330k, an unquantified privacy incident) sum to well over the cap before we consider anything undisclosed. A 20% cap is at the low-to-mid end of the Australian private M&A range for a deal of this size and profile; for a SaaS business whose value is concentrated in IP, data and a few customer contracts, a higher cap (or W&I insurance with a lower retention) is justified.

**Push back:** Cap for general warranties at 30–50% of price as an opening position, or accept 20% only if (i) fundamental, tax and IP warranties and all specific indemnities sit outside the cap (or at 100% of price), and (ii) a retention/escrow secures claims (see Issue 9).

### Issue 2 – De minimis and basket (Cl 12.2)

**Seller position:** AUD 25,000 per claim; AUD 250,000 aggregate; **excess-only (deductible) recovery**.

**Analysis:**
- De minimis of AUD 25k (~0.1% of price) is high-ish but tolerable.
- The basket at ~1% of price is within range, but the **deductible structure** is not the buyer-favourable norm. The more common Australian position is "tipping" (once the basket is exceeded, the whole amount is recoverable).
- Note the drafting risk that "related claims" arising from one set of facts get split to fall under de minimis. Require aggregation of claims arising from the same or related facts.

**Push back:** Tipping basket at AUD 240,000 (1%); de minimis at AUD 10–15k; aggregation language; thresholds not to apply to specific indemnities, fundamental warranties or tax.

### Issue 3 – Time limits and the "all Claims" sweep (Cl 12.3 / 13)

**Seller position:** 18 months for general warranty claims **and** "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise."

**Analysis:** 18 months for general warranties is acceptable (it captures one full audit cycle). The real problem is the default sweep: unless we expressly carve out each category, tax, title/capacity, IP, the specific indemnities and fraud all fall into the 18-month / AUD 4.8m / basket regime. Tax claims routinely surface on an ATO review well beyond 18 months. This drafting shifts the burden of carve-outs onto us and makes any omission fatal.

**Push back:** Reverse the default — limitations apply **only** to general warranty claims unless expressly stated. Separate periods: tax 7 years (or the relevant amendment period + 6 months); fundamental/title 6–7 years (or no limit); IP/data 3–5 years; specific indemnities per their own terms; no limit for fraud, wilful concealment or dishonesty.

### Issue 4 – Fundamental and title warranties subject to general caps

**Seller position:** Capacity and title warranties capped and time-limited like general warranties "for administrative simplicity".

**Analysis:** This is not a market position and there is nothing administrative about it. If title to the shares fails, Wattlebridge has paid AUD 24m for nothing and would be limited to AUD 4.8m recovery within 18 months. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason; it is a transfer of the most basic risk in the deal from Seller to Buyer. Combine this with Issue 12 (title evidenced only by the company's own register) and the exposure is acute.

**Push back:** Non-negotiable. Fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority, no insolvency) capped at 100% of price, excluded from basket/de minimis, with a 6+ year limitation period or none.

### Issue 5 – Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to "all Claims of any nature" (Cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

**Seller position:** The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions extend to all Claims.

**Analysis:** Read literally this purports to:
- cap and time-bar claims for fraud and wilful misconduct (unenforceable as a matter of public policy as to fraud, but the attempt signals intent and creates litigation friction);
- cap claims under the **specific indemnities** (Ironquay, and any we obtain for Riverlark, DD-006, bonuses) — which defeats their purpose;
- cap claims for breach of **covenants** (e.g. the gap-period conduct and Completion obligations), which should be uncapped contractual obligations;
- impose exclusive-remedy and non-reliance language that could be argued to cut across statutory claims (ACL s 18 misleading or deceptive conduct). Non-reliance clauses can be effective at narrowing s 18 exposure, so we should not accept broad language casually.

**Push back:** Carve out from all limitations: fraud, wilful misconduct, dishonesty, fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities, covenant breaches, and Seller's Completion obligations. Limit non-reliance to representations *not* set out in the SPA, Disclosure Letter and specifically identified management responses; confirm it does not exclude statutory rights that cannot be excluded.

### Issue 6 – General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Sch 7; DL 1.1–1.2)

**Seller position:** Everything in the data room (DD-002 to DD-012), the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records" is deemed disclosed against all warranties.

**Analysis:**
- Disclosing the entire data room against every warranty effectively converts the warranties into a due-diligence summary and deprives Wattlebridge of protection on anything that could have been inferred from thousands of pages. Australian practice generally accepts data-room disclosure only where the data room is indexed, fixed (USB/encrypted copy agreed at signing), and the disclosure standard is "fair, with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter".
- "Publicly searchable corporate records" is open-ended (ASIC, PPSR, IP Australia, court registers, land titles, Fair Work?) and unbounded in time. It should be limited to specified searches conducted at specified dates, with results annexed.
- The Disclosure Letter is itself careful to say what it does *not* establish (e.g. paras 4, 5, 6, 8, 10). That candour should be turned to our advantage: nothing not specifically and fairly disclosed should be treated as disclosed.

**Push back:** Specific disclosure only, against identified warranties, to a "fair disclosure" standard. If any general data-room disclosure is accepted, restrict to the indexed data room as frozen at an agreed date (updated to signing), with an agreed index and a USB copy signed by both parties; exclude anything that requires inference or cross-referencing of multiple documents to understand (para 8 of the DL — "read together for timing/scope" — is precisely the problem).

### Issue 7 – Buyer-knowledge qualification (Cl 8.3)

**Seller position:** No claim for any matter the Buyer "or its advisers had knowledge" of, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records".

**Analysis:** This is the single most dangerous clause in the package when combined with Issue 6. "Discoverable" is a constructive-knowledge test — the Seller could resist every claim by saying the matter *could* have been found. "Advisers" sweeps in anything a junior at any of our advisory firms saw. It also undermines the purpose of the warranty-indemnity structure: a buyer that knows of a risk and prices accordingly should still be able to allocate that risk contractually (this is why many Australian SPAs include a "no knowledge defence" / anti-sandbagging exclusion in the buyer's favour).

**Push back:** Delete. Fallback: knowledge limited to **actual** knowledge of named individuals (three or four Wattlebridge deal team members), of facts that would reasonably put them on notice that a warranty was untrue, **and** excluding any matter that is the subject of a specific indemnity. No reference to advisers or "discoverable".

### Issue 8 – Bluefen consent (Cl 3 / 6.3; DL para 2)

**Facts:** Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m FY26 revenue (~30% of the business). Contract cl 11.2 contains a change-of-control consent right with conditions in cl 11.3. The DL confirms no final written consent is in the data room and no evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied.

**Seller position:** "Reasonable endeavours" and consent deemed satisfied "on delivery of the counterparty's written consent".

**Analysis:**
- "Reasonable endeavours" is the weakest endeavours standard. Loss of 30% of revenue is a valuation issue, not a workstream.
- "Delivery of the counterparty's written consent" ignores the cl 11.3 conditions. A conditional consent, or one delivered but with conditions unsatisfied, could be argued to satisfy the CP while leaving Bluefen free to terminate.
- No gap-period protection against Bluefen giving notice of non-renewal or price renegotiation.

**Push back:** (i) Unconditional written Bluefen consent, in agreed form, with cl 11.3 conditions satisfied (or waived in writing by Bluefen), as a **Buyer-only** CP; (ii) "all reasonable endeavours" / "best endeavours" on the Seller, with Buyer participation in Bluefen communications; (iii) MAC / termination right if Bluefen gives notice of termination or material reduction; (iv) price adjustment or earn-out protection if the consent is obtained only with commercial concessions; (v) specific indemnity for loss arising from Bluefen termination triggered by the transaction for a defined period post-Completion.

### Issue 9 – Riverlark facility (Cl 2 / 7; DL para 3)

**Facts:** ~AUD 3.2m outstanding; change-of-control cl 8.1; discharge cl 9.2. Not repaid; no discharge of security in the data room.

**Seller position:** Release "to be provided following Completion".

**Analysis:** This is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal and leaves Wattlebridge buying a company (a) in breach of its facility on Completion (cl 8.1 change of control) and (b) with Riverlark's security still over the assets, including presumably the IP. "Following Completion" with no deadline, no funds-flow mechanic and no escrow means we are relying on the Seller to pay a lender after we have paid the Seller.

**Push back:** Standard payoff mechanics: Riverlark payout letter at an agreed date; the payout amount deducted from the price and paid directly to Riverlark at Completion from the Buyer's funds; executed deed of release and PPSR discharge (and any mortgage releases) delivered at Completion as a Completion deliverable; Seller to procure Riverlark's waiver of the cl 8.1 change-of-control breach or confirm repayment satisfies it. Confirm whether Riverlark holds a general security interest over Paperbark's IP — if so, release before or at Completion is essential, not post-Completion.

### Issue 10 – Funds flow and DD-005 closing bonuses (AUD 420,000)

**Facts:** DD-005 shows Completion bonuses of AUD 420k conditional on Completion and continued employment, not in the funds flow, and silent on payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs.

**Seller position:** "A matter for the Seller and not separately itemised."

**Analysis:** The bonuses are a liability of **Paperbark** (the target), triggered by Completion, so unless the price mechanism deducts them they are paid by the company Wattlebridge now owns — i.e. by us. On-costs (super at 12% from 1 July 2025, payroll tax at ~5.45% in NSW, and possibly employer withholding) push the true cost towards AUD 500k. "A matter for the Seller" is only true if the Seller funds them.

**Push back:** Treat the gross bonus amount plus super, payroll tax and all on-costs as Debt (or a Transaction Expense) deducted from the price; or Seller pays them (grossed up) into the company at Completion; funds flow to itemise. Warranty and indemnity that no other change-of-control or transaction payments exist. Also check whether any bonus is conditional on *continued employment post-Completion* — if so, Wattlebridge wants to control retention rather than be stuck with a liability designed by the Seller.

### Issue 11 – Ironquay IP (Cl 11.1; DL para 4)

**Facts:** DD-004 cl 7.3: SOW3 Project Materials only transfer to Paperbark on cleared payment of **every** SOW3 fee. AUD 180k open per DD-010. No receipt, no confirmatory assignment.

**Seller position:** Indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment.

**Analysis:** The Seller's indemnity covers the AUD 180k — but the real risk is that **Paperbark does not own the IP** developed under SOW3 (and, depending on how cl 7.3 is drafted, possibly earlier SOWs). For a SaaS business, that is a title-to-assets issue, not a payables issue. Paying AUD 180k fixes it only if the assignment then follows automatically; the DL admits no confirmatory assignment exists. The DL's caveat that DD-010 is "not independent bank verification of non-payment" is unhelpful — it signals the Seller may dispute the quantum later.

**Push back:** (i) Completion deliverable: evidence of cleared payment of all SOW fees **and** an executed confirmatory IP assignment from Ironquay to Paperbark (with moral-rights consents) in agreed form; (ii) specific indemnity covering all loss arising from any defect in Paperbark's title to any Ironquay-developed materials, not limited to the SOW3 fee, outside the cap/basket; (iii) IP warranties to expressly cover all contractor-developed code; (iv) ask whether any Paperbark platform code was developed by other contractors on similar terms.

### Issue 12 – DD-006 data export / privacy incident (Cl 4.6 / Sch 6; DL para 6)

**Facts:** Download link sent to an unintended external address; ~1,240 records of names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps; investigation "preliminary"; no determination on access, scope or notification.

**Seller position:** "Preliminary operational matter… not expected to be material."

**Analysis:**
- Under the Privacy Act (Notifiable Data Breaches scheme), the assessment obligation is to be completed within 30 days of becoming aware of a suspected eligible data breach. The incident was known before 22 September; it is now 5 November. If the assessment is still "preliminary", Paperbark may already be in breach of its assessment obligation, and the failure to notify affected individuals/OAIC (if required) would be a continuing contravention we inherit.
- "Business emails/roles" does not necessarily take the data outside "personal information". Customer contractual obligations (including under Bluefen's contract) may impose separate notification obligations and termination rights regardless of the Privacy Act outcome.
- The Seller's characterisation ("not expected to be material") is not a disclosure of fact; the DL (para 6) itself refuses to characterise it.

**Push back:** (i) Immediate request for the investigation report, access logs from the link host, confirmation of link revocation and any OAIC/customer correspondence; (ii) pre-signing CP or covenant: completion of the assessment and any required notifications; (iii) specific indemnity for all loss from the incident (regulatory penalties, remediation, customer claims, Bluefen termination), uncapped or capped at price, outside basket, 6-year period; (iv) warranty that no other actual or suspected data breaches exist; (v) consider whether a cyber/privacy legal review of the platform is warranted before signing.

### Issue 13 – Sandbar supplier renewals (AUD 330,000; DL para 8)

**Facts:** Three related renewals of AUD 110k each across DD-008 and DD-011; the DL will not say whether they are avoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Seller position:** Ordinary-course operating costs.

**Analysis:** The splitting into three AUD 110k items across two documents is curious — it keeps each item under what may be an approval threshold or a materiality figure in the warranties. If these are committed non-cancellable amounts that fall due around or after Completion, they are working-capital/debt-like items for the price mechanism. The Seller's refusal to characterise them in the DL contradicts the Update's "ordinary course" label.

**Push back:** Require the Seller to state in the DL whether each renewal is committed, cancellable, pre-paid or accrued, and whether the services are still required; treat committed non-cancellable amounts not reflected in working capital as Debt; gap-period covenant restricting new supplier commitments above an aggregate (not per-item) threshold.

### Issue 14 – Tax and IP warranties "settled under the general regime"

**Analysis:** This means tax and IP sit under the 20% cap, 18-month period, basket and buyer-knowledge qualifier. Tax exposure in a target routinely emerges on ATO review after 18 months; IP is the asset we are buying. Neither should be in the general bucket.

**Push back:** Separate tax indemnity (full, for all pre-Completion tax, outside the cap/basket, 7-year period, no knowledge defence). IP warranties with a longer period and higher cap; ownership of platform IP ideally a fundamental warranty.

### Issue 15 – Title verification (DL para 10)

**Facts:** The only title evidence is Paperbark's own share register (DD-012), and the DL expressly notes the Buyer has not done its own verification.

**Analysis:** A company's own register is maintained by the company and can be wrong. Combined with Issue 4 (fundamental warranties under the general cap) this is a real gap.

**Push back:** Independent ASIC company extract and historical extract at signing and Completion; review of the chain of share transfers; confirm no options, convertibles, pre-emption rights or shareholder agreements; PPSR search against the shares (Riverlark may have security over them); fundamental title warranty at 100% cap (Issue 4).

### Issue 16 – Lease and Mossvale (DL paras 7 and 9)

**Lease (DD-007):** Notification obligation only. Confirm the clause does not have consequences for failure to notify (e.g. landlord termination right); make notification a Completion deliverable.

**Mossvale (DD-009):** Restriction on assignment — the DL correctly notes a share sale is not an assignment. Confirm there is no change-of-control provision elsewhere in the contract and that nothing in the deal structure (e.g. a post-Completion integration or novation to a Wattlebridge entity) would trigger it. Low priority unless Mossvale is a material customer or supplier.

---

## 3. Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Seller position | Recommended Buyer position | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Preamble / "FINAL" labelling | Positions settled, not to be reopened | Confirm with principals; otherwise treat all as open | Immediate |
| 2 | Disclosure Letter date | 22 Sep 2026 | Bring-down disclosure and updated data room at signing and Completion | Immediate |
| 3 | Riverlark AUD 3.2m | Release post-Completion | Payoff at Completion from price; deed of release and PPSR discharge as Completion deliverable | Critical |
| 4 | Fundamental/title warranties | Under general cap and 18 months | 100% of price cap; 6+ year period; outside basket | Critical |
| 5 | Buyer-knowledge (Cl 8.3) | Constructive, incl. advisers and "discoverable" | Delete; fallback actual knowledge of named individuals only, excl. indemnified matters | Critical |
| 6 | Bluefen consent | Reasonable endeavours; any written consent | Buyer-only CP; unconditional consent with cl 11.3 satisfied; all-reasonable endeavours; MAC/termination right; indemnity | Critical |
| 7 | "All Claims" sweep (Cl 12.3/13, 9.3/12.8/20.5) | Limitations apply to everything by default | Reverse default; carve out fraud, fundamental, tax, specific indemnities, covenants | Critical |
| 8 | Liability cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m | 30–50% opening, or 20% with carve-outs + escrow/W&I | High |
| 9 | Basket | AUD 250k deductible | AUD 240k tipping; AUD 10–15k de minimis; aggregation of related claims | High |
| 10 | General disclosure | Entire data room + public records | Specific fair disclosure only; frozen indexed data room if any general disclosure | High |
| 11 | DD-006 privacy incident | "Not expected to be material" | Full investigation materials; NDB assessment completed pre-signing; specific uncapped indemnity | High |
| 12 | Ironquay IP | Indemnity for SOW3 fee only | Payment + confirmatory assignment as Completion deliverable; indemnity for title defect, not just the fee | High |
| 13 | DD-005 bonuses AUD 420k | "Matter for the Seller", not in funds flow | Gross amount + super/payroll tax/on-costs deducted as Debt; itemised in funds flow | High |
| 14 | Tax and IP | Under general regime | Separate tax indemnity (7 yrs, uncapped); IP warranties elevated | High |
| 15 | Title verification | Company register only | Independent ASIC and PPSR searches; chain-of-title review | Medium |
| 16 | Sandbar renewals AUD 330k | "Ordinary course" | Seller to characterise each; committed amounts treated as Debt; aggregate gap-period threshold | Medium |
| 17 | Lease / Mossvale | Notification only / no consent | Notification as Completion deliverable; confirm no CoC clause in Mossvale | Low |

**Suggested escrow / retention:** Given the concentration of known exposures (Bluefen, Riverlark, DD-006, Ironquay, bonuses) and the Seller's resistance on caps, recommend an escrow of at least AUD 2.4–3.6m (10–15% of price) for 18–24 months, with specific holdbacks against the Bluefen and DD-006 matters released on satisfaction of agreed milestones. Alternatively, obtain W&I insurance quotes now — the Seller's 20% cap would be workable if backed by a policy, but note insurers will likely exclude the known matters (DD-006, Ironquay, Riverlark), which reinforces the need for specific indemnities on those.

**Immediate actions:**
1. Confirm with Wattlebridge principals what, if anything, was actually agreed on Clauses 8, 12 and 13.
2. Request updated data room, bring-down DL, Bluefen consent status, Riverlark payout letter, Ironquay payment/assignment status, and the DD-006 investigation report.
3. Run independent ASIC, PPSR, IP Australia and court searches against Paperbark and Harbourglass.
4. Instruct financial DD to confirm whether bonuses, on-costs and Sandbar commitments are reflected in the working capital/debt definitions.

This note is a legal issues analysis based solely on the Seller's documents as provided; it should be read with the full SPA draft, the underlying DD-002 to DD-012 documents and the financial/tax DD reports before positions are communicated to the Seller.
=== END ADVICE ===
